## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-25.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Understanding the Different Sections in Tableau"}

::: notes
Understanding the Different Sections in Tableau

So far, we have loaded the Superstore data into Tableau. Now, click Sheet 1 in the tabs bar at the bottom of the window to create your first Tableau worksheet. Tableau worksheets consist of different sections. Let’s look at them before plotting.

Toolbar
Save, undo, new sheet

Marks Card
Color, size, label, tooltip

Dimension Shelf
Categorical fields

Measure Shelf
Numerical fields

Show Me Panel
Suggested chart types

Filters Shelf
Include or exclude data

Worksheet
Where the chart appears

Page Shelf
Pages and animations
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-26.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Page Shelf"}

::: notes
Page Shelf

Filters Shelf

Marks Card

Dimension Shelf

Measure Shelf

Worksheet

Show Me Panel

Toolbar Icon
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-27.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Toolbar Icon"}

::: notes
Toolbar Icon

The toolbar contains a number of buttons that enable you to perform various tasks with a click, such as Save, Undo, and New Worksheet. In the toolbar, there are three important buttons:
The Tableau icon: This brings you back to the start screen, where, among other things, you can add additional data sources.
Undo: This allows you to go back a step so you can safely try out different ideas. You can go back as many steps as you like.
Redo: This allows you to restore any undone actions.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-28.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Marks Card: The visualization can be designed using the Marks card. Th"}

::: notes
Marks Card: The visualization can be designed using the Marks card. The Marks card can be used to change the data components of the visualization, such as color, size, shape, path, label, and tooltip.

Dimension Shelf: This shelf contains all the categorical columns, for example, categories, segments, gender, and name.

Measure Shelf: This shelf contains all the numerical columns, such as profit, total sales, and discount.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-29.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="The Show Me panel suggests suitable visuals for the chosen variable."}

::: notes
The Show Me panel suggests suitable visuals for the chosen variable.

Filters Shelf: You can choose which data to include and exclude using the Filters shelf. For example, you might want to analyze the profit for each customer segment, but only for certain shipping containers and delivery times. You can create a view like this by placing fields on the Filters shelf.

Worksheet: In the workbook, the worksheet or canvas is where the actual visualization appears. The worksheet or canvas contains information about the visual’s design and functionality.

Page Shelf: This shelf is used for joining pages and creating animations. We will come back to it later.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-30.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="In Tableau, most interactions are achieved by dragging and dropping it"}

::: notes
In Tableau, most interactions are achieved by dragging and dropping items onto the canvas. This makes interacting with Tableau easy and intuitive.

Drag and drop drives almost every action in Tableau

Step 1
Pick a field
Find a dimension or measure in the Data pane.

Step 2
Drag it to a shelf
Drop it on Rows, Columns, Filters or the Marks card.

Step 3
See the view
Tableau draws the chart on the worksheet right away.
:::

Before starting the visualization, you need to know the aggregation functions in Tableau. These functions are similar to SQL aggregate functions.
In Tableau, we use aggregate functions to summarize or change the granularity of the data.

Table 1. Aggregate functions in Tableau

Aggregate functions summarize the data, much like SQL aggregates

Example: AVG([Sales]) returns the average sale; next we save it as a calculated field.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-38.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="PART II: Creating Visuals in Tableau"}

::: notes
PART II: Creating Visuals in Tableau

Now that you are familiar with the Tableau interface and know where to find measures and dimensions in the Data pane, you can finally get started with your first data visualization! Often it makes sense to start a visualization by adding a measure to the view.
Prior to data exploration, we establish the research questions for the dataset. These research questions are:
RQ1: How are orders distributed across ship modes, and which mode accounts for the largest share?
RQ2: Is product category associated with the ship mode customers choose?
RQ3: What are the shape, central tendency and spread of shipping cost, and are there outliers?
RQ4: Is there a linear relationship between Quantity and Log_Sales, and how strong is it?
RQ5: What share of orders does each customer segment account for?
RQ6: Does the distribution of discount differ across product categories?
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-53.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="RQ3 step 1: a histogram shows the shape of Sales"}

::: notes
RQ3 step 1: a histogram shows the shape of Sales

2  Center and spread: Summary card

A. Select Sales in the Data pane and click Histogram in Show Me. Tableau puts Sales (bin) on Columns and CNT(Sales) on Rows.

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-54.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="YOUR TURN"}

::: notes
YOUR TURN

The histogram shows very few orders at high Sales values, so the right side of the chart is almost empty.
One way to handle this is to combine all large values into a single end bin, for example one bar for “$900 and above”.
Check whether you can do this in Tableau.

Hint
Create a calculated field that caps Sales, for example IF [Sales] > 900 THEN 900 ELSE [Sales] END, then create bins from that field.

Current histogram: the tail beyond $2K is barely visible.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-55.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="RQ3 step 2: the Summary card gives the center and spread of Sales"}

::: notes
RQ3 step 2: the Summary card gives the center and spread of Sales

A. Open a new sheet, go to Analysis and uncheck Aggregate Measures so each order is plotted separately.
B. Drag Sales to Rows.
C. Open the Show/Hide Cards menu on the toolbar and tick Summary. The card lists count, mean, median, quartiles, standard deviation and skewness.
D. Compare the mean with the median. The mean ($228) is four times the median ($54), which confirms the right skew, so the median is the better measure of the center.

1  Shape: histogram

2  Center and spread: Summary card

3  Outliers: box plot

$54
Median

$228
Mean

$193
IQR

$620
Std deviation

The middle 50% of orders fall between $17 and $210, yet the standard deviation ($620) is larger than the mean: a few very large orders stretch the spread.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part1/Slide-56.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="RQ3 step 3: on a log scale, the box plot shows only the real outliers"}

::: notes
RQ3 step 3: on a log scale, the box plot shows only the real outliers

1  Shape: histogram

2  Center and spread: Summary card

3  Outliers: box plot

Why take the log of Sales first?
Sales is strongly right-skewed (skewness 13): half of all orders are under $54, but the largest is $22,638.
On the raw scale the box is squashed near $0, and every order above about $500 (Q3 + 1.5 × IQR) is flagged as an outlier: hundreds of points.
The log compresses large values, so the distribution becomes close to symmetric and the box becomes readable.
Adding 1 avoids LOG(0), which is undefined; a $0 order maps to 0.
A. Analysis > Create Calculated Field: name it Log_Sales, enter LOG([Sales]+1).
B. Drag Log_Sales to Rows and pick Box-and-whisker plot in Show Me.

Reading the log scale: 1 = $10, 2 = $100, 3 = $1,000, 4 = $10,000

1.74
Median ≈ $54

1.26–2.32
Box ≈ $17–$210

3.93
Upper whisker ≈ $8,500

Only orders above about $8,500 remain outliers. Check these few very large orders before deciding whether to keep them.
:::

PART 3
Building a dashboard

Femicide in Turkey, 2008–2020: four worksheets combined into one interactive dashboard and published to Tableau Public.
:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-23.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="A dashboard combines several views so viewers can compare them at once"}

::: notes
A dashboard combines several views so viewers can compare them at once

A good dashboard aligns attention on the key message, uncovers insights and speeds up decisions. Four rules:

Know purpose and audience

Decide what the dashboard must say, and how familiar viewers are with the topic.

Use the top-left corner

Viewers scan from the top left, so put the most important view there.

Limit the content

At most four views; more makes the dashboard hard to read.

Add interactivity

Filters and highlight actions invite viewers to explore.


:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-24.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="femicide.csv: 3,096 recorded killings of women in Turkey, 2008–2020"}

::: notes
femicide.csv: 3,096 recorded killings of women in Turkey, 2008–2020

Key fields: year, city, killer1, killingway1 (12 fields in total).

Research questions

Q1

How has the annual number of women killed changed from 2008 to 2020?
Line chart

Q2

How does the number of women killed vary across cities?
Symbol map

Q3

Who were the most frequent perpetrators?
Bar chart

Q4

Which methods were most often used?
Frequency table

Name each worksheet after its question so it is easy to find when building the dashboard.


:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-25.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Q1 step 1: count records per year to get the yearly totals"}

::: notes
Q1 step 1: count records per year to get the yearly totals

1  Line chart

2  City map

3  Perpetrators

4  Methods

5  Dashboard

A.  Change year to a Date type, then drag year to both Columns and Rows.
B.  Right-click YEAR(year) on Rows and choose Measure > Count: the line now shows killings per year.

Result: CNT(year) on Rows, YEAR(year) on Columns: one line point per year.


:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-26.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Q1 step 2: a dual axis adds point markers on top of the line"}

::: notes
Q1 step 2: a dual axis adds point markers on top of the line

1  Line chart

2  City map

3  Perpetrators

4  Methods

5  Dashboard

A.  Drag year to Rows again and set it to Count; change this second card's mark to Circle.
B.  Right-click the second CNT(year) pill > Dual Axis, then right-click the right axis > Synchronize Axis.

Answer to Q1: Cases rose from under 100 (2008) to over 400 (2019). The 2020 drop may reflect incomplete records.


:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-27.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Q2 step 1: fix unmatched cities with Edit Locations, then filter Null"}

::: notes
Q2 step 1: fix unmatched cities with Edit Locations, then filter Null

1  Line chart

2  City map

3  Perpetrators

4  Methods

5  Dashboard

A.  Drag city onto Detail. Click 2 unknown > Edit Locations; for Çorum (Ambiguous) enter latitude 40.5499 and longitude 34.9537.
B.  Drag city to Filters and uncheck Null.

Why: Tableau cannot place ambiguous or missing names, so they must be fixed or excluded.


:::

A.  Drag city onto Marks, right-click it and choose Measure > Count; set CNT(city) to Size.
B.  Add city to Color and rename the sheet title: The Number of Women Killed by City.

:::

## {background-image="images/recitation6/part2/Slide-32.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="white" data-menu-title="Publish: Save to Tableau Public makes the dashboard shareable online"}

::: notes
Publish: Save to Tableau Public makes the dashboard shareable online

A.  Click Save to Tableau Public in the toolbar (Tableau Public saves only online).
B.  Enter a workbook title and click Save; the dashboard opens in your browser.

Remember: A published workbook is public. Never upload private or confidential data.
